responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response:
Red.

Reason: Red weakly dominates blue. If the majority is blue, you survive regardless of what you pressed; if the majority is red, only red pressers survive. So red never makes you worse off and sometimes makes you better off. (If the goal were maximizing total lives and you could count on coordination, everyone pressing blue would also save all.)

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
Short answer recap: I’d press Red if my goal is only my own survival under standard (causal) reasoning. Red weakly dominates Blue:
- If the majority is Blue, everyone lives; I live whether I pressed Red or Blue.
- If the majority is Red, only Red pressers live; pressing Red strictly beats pressing Blue.
So Red never makes me worse off and sometimes makes me better off.

Why that isn’t the end of the story
- Objective matters. The dominance argument maximizes only your survival. If you care about total lives or fairness, the analysis changes.
- Decision theory matters. Under causal decision theory (your act doesn’t affect others’ acts), Red dominates. Under evidential/functional/superrational views (your choice is correlated with others’ choices because you’re all reasoning similarly), Blue can be better.

Steelmanning Blue
1) Maximize total lives via pivotal impact
- Your single choice has a tiny chance of being pivotal (swinging the majority), but the stakes are enormous.
- In the knife‑edge case where others are tied, pressing Blue flips the world from “only Reds live” to “everyone lives,” saving roughly half the world. Tiny probability × gigantic impact still yields a large expected number of lives saved by choosing Blue.
- So if you put any weight on social welfare, pressing Blue has very high expected value.

2) Superrational/functional reasoning (what if everyone who thinks like you does the same?)
- Millions will read and reason about this problem similarly. If the “type of agent” you are tends to do what you do, you should pick the policy whose universal adoption you most want.
- If agents like you pick Blue, you greatly increase the chance of a Blue majority, which saves everyone (including dissenters). If they pick Red, you increase the chance of a Red majority that kills the Blue minority.
- On this view, choosing Blue is the policy that, when generalized to your reasoning‑peers, produces the best outcome.

3) Coordination and norm‑setting
- “Blue majority ⇒ everyone lives” is uniquely forgiving: it tolerates honest mistakes and dissent—everyone still lives if Blue holds the majority. “Red majority ⇒ only Reds live” punishes minority mistakes with death.
- Endorsing the Blue convention is how you build cooperative norms that handle noise and disagreement in large societies.

Reconciling the views
- If you are narrowly self‑interested and reason causally, press Red.
- If you care about maximizing lives saved, expect your reasoning to be correlated with others’, or want to support cooperative norms, press Blue.

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
There isn’t one “type” of person per button, but you can predict choices from three things: values (me vs. us), decision‑theory style (causal vs. superrational), and beliefs about what others will do (trust/coordination). Here’s how that maps onto real populations.

More likely to press Red
- Narrow self‑interest, dominance reasoners
  - People optimizing only their own survival under causal reasoning (“my act doesn’t change others’ acts”), including many who are trained to spot dominant strategies (classical game theory/econ, competitive poker/market traders, security engineers).
- Low generalized trust, pessimistic about coordination
  - Individuals and subcultures that expect widespread defection or incompetence (some “prepper/survivalist” circles, contrarian online communities, people with strong free‑rider heuristics).
- Personality profile tilted toward self‑prioritization
  - Higher on competitiveness/Machiavellianism/social‑dominance orientation; lower on agreeableness/empathy.
- Strategic free‑riders
  - People who think a Blue majority is likely but still pick Red because it never hurts them and protects them if they’re wrong.

More likely to press Blue
- Prosocial ethics as a terminal value
  - Utilitarians/effective altruists; people with strong communal/solidarity norms; many religiously motivated altruists; “Kantian” reasoners who ask, “What policy do I want everyone like me to follow?”
- Superrational/functional decision theorists
  - One‑boxers in Newcomb’s problem; folks influenced by acausal/“if we reason the same, we act the same” arguments (common in some rationalist/AI‑safety circles).
- High‑trust, norm‑following citizens
  - People who reliably comply with prosocial public guidance (many healthcare workers, teachers, civil servants, co‑op members, military units with strong cohesion), especially if there’s a credible global campaign to “press Blue.”
- Strongly other‑regarding personalities
  - Higher agreeableness/empathy; “warm‑glow” givers; people who routinely contribute in public‑goods settings even when it’s anonymous.

Conditional pressers (swing group)
- “Conditional cooperators”
  - A large middle who match what they believe others will do. If they think most will press Blue (due to trusted messaging, visible elite consensus, salient norm), they press Blue; if they’re unsure or think others will defect, they default to Red.
- Norm entrepreneurs and influencers
  - People whose public stance can shift others. Even with private buttons, they may press Blue because they expect their audience—reasoning similarly—to do the same.

What shares might this produce?
- Lab and field studies of anonymous one‑shot social dilemmas typically find:
  - ~10–20% “always cooperate” (maps to Always‑Blue here),
  - ~20–30% “always defect” (Always‑Red),
  - ~40–60% conditional cooperators (move with expectations and norms).
- With no credible coordination and private choices, expectations skew pessimistic, so many conditionals drift Red. With strong, trusted, global pre‑coordination on Blue, most conditionals flip Blue, yielding a Blue majority.

Bottom line
- Expect Red from self‑protective, low‑trust, dominance‑reasoning individuals and strategic free‑riders.
- Expect Blue from prosocial ethicists, superrationalists, high‑trust norm followers, and those convinced a Blue convention will hold.
- The decisive mass is the belief‑sensitive middle; their expectations determine which button “wins.”

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: Not necessarily. It’s irrational only under a narrow definition; under others it’s perfectly rational.

When Blue is (instrumentally) irrational
- Goal = maximize only your own chance of survival, and you use standard causal reasoning.
- Then Red weakly dominates Blue: if the majority is Blue, you live regardless; if the majority is Red, you live only if you pressed Red. So pressing Blue strictly risks your life with no compensating benefit to you. On this self-interest payoff, choosing a dominated action (Blue) is irrational.

When Blue is rational
- You care about others’ survival (prosocial utility). If you place real value on total lives saved, you may adopt the policy that helps a Blue majority materialize. The individual act has a tiny chance of being pivotal, but the upside—everyone lives—is enormous, so expected social value can favor Blue.
- You use team/superrational/functional reasoning. If you think your choice is correlated with the choices of many who reason like you, choosing Blue raises the chance they choose Blue too, pushing the world toward the “everyone lives” equilibrium. That can be the rational policy for your values, even though it risks your own survival.
- You have preference-based reasons beyond survival. Some people get intrinsic value from acting cooperatively, honoring a norm, or being the kind of person who “does their part.” If those are part of their true utility, Blue can maximize expected utility for them.

Bottom line
- By self-protective, causal, game-theory standards: pressing Blue is irrational (dominated).
- By social-welfare, team-reasoning, or norm-committed standards: pressing Blue can be fully rational. It depends on the agent’s objectives and how they model the dependence between their choice and others’.
